title: Χάρυβδις, Θρινακίη καὶ Σειρῆνες
titleEn: Charybdis, the Sun’s Cattle and the Sirens’ Song — Odyssey 12.101–191
part: Charybdis, the Sun’s Cattle and the Sirens’ Song (12.101–191)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Circe finishes her counsel. The second crag is lower and bears a wild fig tree; beneath it Charybdis sucks down the dark water three times a day, and not even the earth-shaker could save a man there, so Odysseus is to keep close to Scylla’s crag and lose six men rather than all. Asked whether he can ward Scylla off, Circe says she is an immortal evil, tells him to flee, and bids him call on her mother Crataeis. Next comes the island of Thrinacia, where the Sun’s cattle and sheep neither breed nor die and are herded by two nymphs: harm them and ship and men are lost, and Odysseus, if he escapes, will come home late and alone. At dawn Circe leaves, the men sail with the wind she sends, and Odysseus tells them what they need to know of the Sirens. In a dead calm off the Sirens’ island he stops the men’s ears with wax and is bound to the mast; as the ship comes within shouting distance the Sirens begin to sing, offering him knowledge of all that was done at Troy and all that happens on earth.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἕτερον σκόπελον χθαμαλώτερον ὄψει, Ὀδυσσεῦ.
sentences.tr: ton d’ heteron skopelon chthamalōteron opsei, Odysseu.
sentences.l: And the other crag lower you will see, Odysseus.
sentences.i: As for the other crag, you will see that it is lower, Odysseus.
sentences.n: Circe’s speech, which opened at 12.37, is still running, so the English opens no new mark. τὸν δ’ ἕτερον σκόπελον is ‘and the other crag’, the object of ὄψει, the second singular future middle of ὁράω (Attic ὄψῃ). χθαμαλώτερον, ‘lower’, is the comparative of χθαμαλός ‘low-lying’, a word built on the idea of the ground (compare χθών ‘earth’); it agrees with σκόπελον as what Odysseus will see. Ὀδυσσεῦ is the vocative.

sentences.t: πλησίον ἀλλήλων·
sentences.tr: plēsion allēlōn·
sentences.l: Near to one another;
sentences.i: They stand near one another;
sentences.n: πλησίον is the adverb ‘near’, here taking the genitive ἀλλήλων ‘of one another’, so the two crags stand close together. The verb ‘are’ is left out, as it often is in Homer’s descriptions. The unit is the short clause that ends at the raised point; the next unit begins in the middle of this same line.

sentences.t: καί κεν διοϊστεύσειας.
sentences.tr: kai ken dioïsteuseias.
sentences.l: and you could even shoot an arrow across.
sentences.i: and you could even shoot an arrow across.
sentences.n: καί κεν … διοϊστεύσειας is a potential optative with κεν, ‘you could even shoot across’. διοϊστεύω is ὀιστεύω ‘shoot an arrow’ (from ὀιστός ‘arrow’) with διά ‘across, through’; no object is given, so the gap between the two crags is understood. καί is ‘even’. The unit begins in the middle of the line, after the raised point that closed the one before.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἐν ἐρινεὸς ἔστι μέγας, φύλλοισι τεθηλώς·
sentences.tr: tōi d’ en erineos esti megas, phylloisi tethēlōs·
sentences.l: And on it a wild fig tree is, great, flourishing with leaves;
sentences.i: And on it there is a great wild fig tree, flourishing with leaves;
sentences.n: τῷ is the dative of the pronoun, ‘on that one’, that is the second crag, and ἐν is an adverb, ‘in it, on it’. ἐρινεός is the wild fig tree, a masculine noun, so μέγας agrees with it. τεθηλώς is the perfect participle of θάλλω ‘bloom, flourish’, with the dative φύλλοισι ‘with leaves’ saying what it flourishes in.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ὑπὸ δῖα Χάρυβδις ἀναρροιβδεῖ μέλαν ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ hypo dia Charybdis anarroibdei melan hydōr.
sentences.l: and beneath it heavenly Charybdis sucks down the dark water.
sentences.i: and beneath it heavenly Charybdis sucks down the dark water.
sentences.n: Charybdis is named here. δῖα is the stock epithet ‘heavenly’, translated as always even though it sits oddly on a monster. ὑπό ‘beneath’ stands after the τῷ it governs. ἀναρροιβδεῖ is from ἀναρροιβδέω ‘swallow down again’, a verb built on ῥοῖβδος, the rushing noise of water. μέλαν ὕδωρ is ‘dark water’; μέλαν is the neuter accusative of μέλας.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μὲν γάρ τ’ ἀνίησιν ἐπ’ ἤματι, τρὶς δ’ ἀναροιβδεῖ
δεινόν·
sentences.tr:
tris men gar t’ aniēsin ep’ ēmati, tris d’ anaroibdei
deinon·
sentences.l:
For three times in a day she sends it up, and three times she sucks it down
dreadfully;
sentences.i: For three times a day she sends it up, and three times she sucks it down, dreadfully;
sentences.n: τρὶς … τρὶς ‘three times … three times’ balance ἀνίησιν ‘she sends up’ (ἀνίημι, with the water understood) and ἀναροιβδεῖ ‘she sucks down’, spelled here with one ρ and in the line before with two: it is the same verb. ἐπ’ ἤματι is ‘in the course of a day’, and the τ’ after γάρ is epic τε. δεινόν is an adverb, ‘dreadfully’. The unit stops at the raised point after δεινόν.

sentences.t: μὴ σύ γε κεῖθι τύχοις, ὅτε ῥοιβδήσειεν·
sentences.tr: mē sy ge keithi tychois, hote rhoibdēseien·
sentences.l: may you at least not be there, when she gulps it down;
sentences.i: may you not be there when she gulps it down;
sentences.n: μὴ σύ γε κεῖθι τύχοις is a wish with μή, ‘may you not be there’: τύχοις is the aorist optative of τυγχάνω ‘happen to be’, κεῖθι is ‘there’ (an old form of ἐκεῖθι), and σύ γε is ‘you, at any rate’. ὅτε ῥοιβδήσειεν is ‘when she gulps down’, ῥοιβδέω being the plain verb under ἀναρροιβδέω; the optative in the time-clause hangs on the wish. The unit begins in the middle of line 106.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ κεν ῥύσαιτό σ’ ὑπὲκ κακοῦ οὐδ’ ἐνοσίχθων.
sentences.tr: ou gar ken rhysaito s’ hypek kakou oud’ enosichthōn.
sentences.l: for he could not rescue you from under the evil, not even the earth-shaker.
sentences.i: for not even the earth-shaker could rescue you out of that trouble.
sentences.n: κεν with the optative ῥύσαιτο is ‘could rescue’; ῥύομαι ‘draw out of danger’ takes σ’ (σε) as its object. ὑπὲκ κακοῦ is ‘out from under evil’: ὑπέκ ‘out from under’ governs the genitive, and κακόν is the neuter ‘evil, trouble’. ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’ is a title of Poseidon, whom Circe does not name here; οὐδ’ is ‘not even’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλα Σκύλλης σκοπέλῳ πεπλημένος ὦκα
νῆα παρὲξ ἐλάαν, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτερόν ἐστιν
ἓξ ἑτάρους ἐν νηὶ ποθήμεναι ἢ ἅμα πάντας.
sentences.tr:
alla mala Skyllēs skopelōi peplēmenos ōka
nēa parex elaan, epei ē poly pherteron estin
hex hetarous en nēi pothēmenai ē hama pantas.
sentences.l:
But very close to Scylla’s crag, drawn near, quickly
the ship drive past, for truly much better it is
to miss six companions in the ship than all together.’
sentences.i: But keep very close to Scylla’s crag, and drive the ship quickly past; for it is truly much better to miss six of your companions from the ship than all of them together.’
sentences.n: Circe’s speech, opened at 12.37, ends with this unit: the next line is the narrator’s. πεπλημένος is the perfect participle of πελάζω ‘bring near’, passive in form with a middle sense, ‘having drawn close up to’, with the dative σκοπέλῳ. ἐλάαν is the uncontracted infinitive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’ used as a command, as παρεξελάαν was earlier. ἦ is ‘truly’, while the ἢ near the end of line 110 is ‘than’. ποθήμεναι is the infinitive in -μεναι of ποθέω ‘miss, long for’, and φέρτερον is ‘better’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar egō min ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: The narrator’s line closes Circe’s speech and opens Odysseus’s reply. ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so she spoke’, with ἔφατο elided; ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον is ‘answering, I addressed’, and μιν is ‘her’. The whole line is the one that stood at 4.375, and it takes the English already given there.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄγε δή μοι τοῦτο, θεά, νημερτὲς ἐνίσπες,
εἴ πως τὴν ὀλοὴν μὲν ὑπεκπροφύγοιμι Χάρυβδιν,
τὴν δέ κ’ ἀμυναίμην, ὅτε μοι σίνοιτό γ’ ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
ei d’ age dē moi touto, thea, nēmertes enispes,
ei pōs tēn oloēn men hypekprophygoimi Charybdin,
tēn de k’ amynaimēn, hote moi sinoito g’ hetairous.
sentences.i: ‘But come now, goddess, tell me this without error: whether I might somehow escape deadly Charybdis, and yet ward off the other when she harms my companions.’
sentences.n: Odysseus asks Circe. εἰ δ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and ἐνίσπες is a form of the aorist of ἐνέπω ‘tell’, the verb of the poem’s first line, serving as the command; νημερτές ‘without error’ is an adverb. One εἴ clause holds both optatives, ὑπεκπροφύγοιμι and ἀμυναίμην (the latter with κ’), joined by μέν … δέ (τὴν ὀλοὴν μὲν … τὴν δέ, ‘the one … the other’); it is an indirect question: ‘whether I might escape … and ward off’. ὑπεκπροφύγοιμι is ‘escape out from under’, ὀλοήν ‘deadly’, and σίνοιτο is from σίνομαι ‘harm’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ἡ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, hē d’ autik’ ameibeto dia theaōn·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and she at once answered, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: So I said, and she, heavenly even among goddesses, answered at once:
sentences.n: The narrator’s line introducing Circe’s answer. ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’ (imperfect middle of φημί), ἀμείβετο ‘answered’, and δῖα θεάων is the stock phrase for a goddess, ‘heavenly even among goddesses’. The whole line occurred at 4.382, and the English given to it there is kept.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιε, καὶ δὴ αὖ τοι πολεμήια ἔργα μέμηλε
καὶ πόνος·
sentences.tr:
schetlie, kai dē au toi polemēia erga memēle
kai ponos·
sentences.l:
‘Cruel one, and so again to you the works of war are a care
and toil;
sentences.i: ‘Cruel one, so once more it is deeds of war and toil that concern you;
sentences.n: Circe answers. σχέτλιε, ‘Cruel one’, is the house rendering, though the word is nearer dismay than cruelty. καὶ δὴ αὖ is ‘and now again’, τοι is ‘to you’, and πολεμήια ἔργα ‘works of war’ with καὶ πόνος ‘and toil’ are the things that are a care to you: μέμηλε is the perfect of μέλω ‘be a care to’, singular because it agrees with the neuter plural ἔργα (which takes a singular verb) and with the singular πόνος. The unit stops at the raised point in line 117.

sentences.t: οὐδὲ θεοῖσιν ὑπείξεαι ἀθανάτοισιν;
sentences.tr: oude theoisin hypeixeai athanatoisin;
sentences.l: and not even to gods will you give way, to immortal ones?
sentences.i: will you not give way even to the immortal gods?
sentences.n: οὐδὲ θεοῖσιν ὑπείξεαι ἀθανάτοισιν is a rhetorical question, ‘will you not yield even to gods?’, with οὐδέ meaning ‘not even’. ὑπείξεαι is the future middle of ὑπείκω ‘give way, yield’, taking the dative, and ἀθανάτοισιν ‘immortal’ is added after the noun for emphasis. The unit begins in the middle of line 117, after the raised point.

sentences.t:
ἡ δέ τοι οὐ θνητή, ἀλλ’ ἀθάνατον κακόν ἐστι,
δεινόν τ’ ἀργαλέον τε καὶ ἄγριον οὐδὲ μαχητόν·
sentences.tr:
hē de toi ou thnētē, all’ athanaton kakon esti,
deinon t’ argaleon te kai agrion oude machēton·
sentences.l:
And she indeed is not mortal, but an immortal evil is,
dread and grievous and savage and not to be fought;
sentences.i: And she is no mortal, but an immortal evil, dread and grievous and savage, and not to be fought against;
sentences.n: ἡ δέ is ‘and she’, that is Scylla (named at 108), and τοι is ‘I tell you’. κακόν is the neuter noun ‘evil’, and δεινόν, ἀργαλέον, ἄγριον and μαχητόν are neuter adjectives agreeing with it: ‘dread’, ‘grievous’, ‘savage’. μαχητόν is the verbal adjective of μάχομαι ‘fight’, ‘fightable’, and οὐδέ negates it.

sentences.t: οὐδέ τις ἔστ’ ἀλκή·
sentences.tr: oude tis est’ alkē·
sentences.l: nor is there any might;
sentences.i: nor is there any might to oppose her;
sentences.n: ἀλκή is ‘might’, the strength to defend oneself or fight back, and οὐδέ τις ἔστ’ ἀλκή is ‘nor is there any might’. ἔστ’ is ἔστι ‘there is’. The thought answers the last unit’s ‘not to be fought’. This short unit ends at the raised point in the middle of line 120; the advice that follows begins the next.

sentences.t: φυγέειν κάρτιστον ἀπ’ αὐτῆς.
sentences.tr: phygeein kartiston ap’ autēs.
sentences.l: to flee is best, away from her.
sentences.i: the best course is to flee from her.
sentences.n: φυγέειν is the uncontracted aorist infinitive of φεύγω (Attic φυγεῖν), the subject of a clause with no verb: ‘to flee is best’. κάρτιστον is the superlative of κρατύς ‘strong’, here ‘best’, and ἀπ’ αὐτῆς is ‘away from her’. The unit begins in the middle of line 120.

sentences.t:
ἢν γὰρ δηθύνῃσθα κορυσσόμενος παρὰ πέτρῃ,
δείδω, μή σ’ ἐξαῦτις ἐφορμηθεῖσα κίχῃσι
τόσσῃσιν κεφαλῇσι, τόσους δ’ ἐκ φῶτας ἕληται.
sentences.tr:
ēn gar dēthynēistha koryssomenos para petrēi,
deidō, mē s’ exautis ephormētheisa kichēisi
tossēisin kephalēisi, tosous d’ ek phōtas helētai.
sentences.l:
For if you linger, arming yourself beside the rock,
I fear lest again, rushing upon you, she reach you
with as many heads, and as many men take out.
sentences.i: For if you stay beside the rock arming yourself, I fear that she may rush upon you again and reach you with as many heads, and take as many men.
sentences.n: ἢν is ἐάν ‘if’, with the subjunctive δηθύνῃσθα (δηθύνω ‘linger’, ending in -σθα) and the participle κορυσσόμενος ‘arming yourself’. δείδω ‘I fear’ takes μή ‘lest’ and the subjunctives κίχῃσι (κιχάνω ‘reach’) and ἕληται, with ἐφορμηθεῖσα ‘having rushed upon’. ἐκ … ἕληται is tmesis for ἐξέληται ‘take out’; ἐξαῦτις is ‘again’. τόσσῃσιν and τόσους ‘as many’ mean the number already in view, six heads and the six companions of line 110.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλα σφοδρῶς ἐλάαν, βωστρεῖν δὲ Κράταιιν,
μητέρα τῆς Σκύλλης, ἥ μιν τέκε πῆμα βροτοῖσιν·
sentences.tr:
alla mala sphodrōs elaan, bōstrein de Krataiin,
mētera tēs Skyllēs, hē min teke pēma brotoisin·
sentences.l:
But very vigorously drive on, and call upon Crataeis,
the mother of Scylla, who bore her, a woe to mortals;
sentences.i: But drive on with all your vigour, and call upon Crataeis, the mother of Scylla, who bore her to be a woe to mortals;
sentences.n: ἐλάαν and βωστρεῖν are infinitives used as commands, ‘drive on’ and ‘call out’; the ship, named with ἐλάαν in line 109, is understood here. μάλα σφοδρῶς is ‘very vehemently’. βωστρέω ‘call on, summon’ takes the accusative Κράταιιν, Crataeis, the mother of Scylla. ἥ μιν τέκε is ‘who bore her’, τέκε unaugmented, and πῆμα ‘woe’ stands in apposition to μιν. The unit stops at the raised point in line 125.

sentences.t: ἥ μιν ἔπειτ’ ἀποπαύσει ἐς ὕστερον ὁρμηθῆναι.
sentences.tr: hē min epeit’ apopausei es hysteron hormēthēnai.
sentences.l: who then will stop her from rushing out hereafter.
sentences.i: and she will then keep her from rushing out later.
sentences.n: ἥ μιν ἔπειτ’ ἀποπαύσει is ‘she will then stop her’: ἥ is the relative continuing the sentence, ἀποπαύσει is the future of ἀποπαύω ‘make stop, hold back’, and μιν is Scylla. ὁρμηθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of ὁρμάω ‘rush out’, and ἐς ὕστερον is ‘afterwards, in time to come’. This ends the advice on the two crags.

sentences.t: Θρινακίην δ’ ἐς νῆσον ἀφίξεαι·
sentences.tr: Thrinakiēn d’ es nēson aphixeai·
sentences.l: And to the island Thrinacia you will come;
sentences.i: And you will come to the island of Thrinacia;
sentences.n: A new paragraph: Circe turns from the two crags to the island of the Sun. Θρινακίην has the Ionic η, ἐς is εἰς ‘to’, and ἀφίξεαι is the future of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive’ (Attic ἀφίξῃ). The unit ends at the raised point in the middle of line 127.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ πολλαὶ
βόσκοντ’ Ἠελίοιο βόες καὶ ἴφια μῆλα,
ἑπτὰ βοῶν ἀγέλαι, τόσα δ’ οἰῶν πώεα καλά,
πεντήκοντα δ’ ἕκαστα.
sentences.tr:
entha de pollai
boskont’ Ēelioio boes kai iphia mēla,
hepta boōn agelai, tosa d’ oiōn pōea kala,
pentēkonta d’ hekasta.
sentences.l:
and there many
graze, of the Sun, cattle and stout flocks,
seven herds of cattle, and as many fine flocks of sheep,
fifty each.
sentences.i: and there graze many cattle of the Sun, and stout flocks: seven herds of cattle, and as many fine flocks of sheep, with fifty in each.
sentences.n: ἔνθα is ‘there’, on Thrinacia. βόσκοντ’ is βόσκονται ‘graze’ with the ending elided, and πολλαί … βόες ‘many cattle’ is feminine plural. ἴφια μῆλα ‘stout flocks’ is the house rendering. ἀγέλαι are ‘herds’ and πώεα ‘flocks’ of sheep (οἰῶν, genitive plural of οἶς), τόσα ‘as many’, and πεντήκοντα … ἕκαστα ‘fifty each’. Ἠελίοιο is the genitive ‘of the Sun’. The unit begins in the middle of line 127 and ends at the full stop in the middle of 130.

sentences.t:
γόνος δ’ οὐ γίγνεται αὐτῶν,
οὐδέ ποτε φθινύθουσι.
sentences.tr:
gonos d’ ou gignetai autōn,
oude pote phthinythousi.
sentences.l:
And offspring of them is not born,
nor do they ever dwindle.
sentences.i: No young are ever born to them, and they never dwindle away.
sentences.n: γόνος is ‘offspring, breeding’, and γόνος … οὐ γίγνεται αὐτῶν is ‘no offspring comes to be of them’, the genitive αὐτῶν being the cattle and sheep. οὐ … οὐδέ ποτε is ‘not … nor ever’. φθινύθουσι is the third plural of φθινύθω, a lengthened form of φθίνω ‘waste away, dwindle’. The unit begins in the middle of line 130.

sentences.t:
θεαὶ δ’ ἐπιποιμένες εἰσίν,
νύμφαι ἐυπλόκαμοι, Φαέθουσά τε Λαμπετίη τε,
ἃς τέκεν Ἠελίῳ Ὑπερίονι δῖα Νέαιρα.
sentences.tr:
theai d’ epipoimenes eisin,
nymphai eyplokamoi, Phaethousa te Lampetiē te,
has teken Ēeliōi Hyperioni dia Neaira.
sentences.l:
And goddesses are their shepherds,
fine-plaited nymphs, Phaethusa and Lampetie,
whom bore to the Sun Hyperion heavenly Neaera.
sentences.i: And goddesses are set over them as shepherds, fine-plaited nymphs, Phaethusa and Lampetie, whom heavenly Neaera bore to the Sun, Hyperion.
sentences.n: ἐπιποιμένες is the plural of ἐπιποιμήν ‘shepherd, one set over flocks’, here used of goddesses. ἐυπλόκαμοι is the house ‘fine-plaited’, and the nymphs’ names, Φαέθουσα and Λαμπετίη, come from verbs of shining. ἃς τέκεν is ‘whom she bore’, the relative accusative plural with unaugmented τέκεν. Ἠελίῳ Ὑπερίονι is ‘to the Sun, to Hyperion’; Hyperion is a name of the Sun here, and at 176 the Sun is called Ὑπεριονίδης ‘son of Hyperion’. δῖα is the stock ‘heavenly’, here of Neaera.

sentences.t:
τὰς μὲν ἄρα θρέψασα τεκοῦσά τε πότνια μήτηρ
Θρινακίην ἐς νῆσον ἀπῴκισε τηλόθι ναίειν,
μῆλα φυλασσέμεναι πατρώια καὶ ἕλικας βοῦς.
sentences.tr:
tas men ara threpsasa tekousa te potnia mētēr
Thrinakiēn es nēson apōikise tēlothi naiein,
mēla phylassemenai patrōia kai helikas bous.
sentences.l:
These indeed, having reared and borne them, their lady mother
to the island Thrinacia settled them away to dwell far off,
to guard their father’s flocks and the crumple-horned cattle.
sentences.i: Their lady mother, when she had reared and borne them, settled them on the island of Thrinacia to live far away, to guard their father’s flocks and the cattle of crumpled horn.
sentences.n: τὰς μὲν ἄρα is ‘these, then’, the nymphs; θρέψασα and τεκοῦσα are aorist participles, ‘having reared and borne’ (the Greek puts them in that order). πότνια μήτηρ is ‘the lady mother’. ἀπῴκισε is the aorist of ἀποικίζω ‘settle away from home’; τηλόθι is ‘far off’. ναίειν and φυλασσέμεναι (an infinitive in -έμεναι) are infinitives of purpose, ‘to live’ and ‘to guard’. πατρώια is ‘their father’s’. ἕλικας is ‘crumple-horned’, from ἕλιξ ‘twisted, curved’, said of βοῦς ‘cattle’.

sentences.t:
τὰς εἰ μέν κ’ ἀσινέας ἐάᾳς νόστου τε μέδηαι,
ἦ τ’ ἂν ἔτ’ εἰς Ἰθάκην κακά περ πάσχοντες ἵκοισθε·
sentences.tr:
tas ei men k’ asineas eaāis nostou te medēai,
ē t’ an et’ eis Ithakēn kaka per paschontes hikoisthe·
sentences.l:
Them, if you leave unharmed and are mindful of the homecoming,
truly you would still reach Ithaca, evils though suffering;
sentences.i: If you leave them unharmed and keep your mind on getting home, you may truly still reach Ithaca, though you suffer hardships;
sentences.n: τάς is the herds and flocks, object of ἐάᾳς, the subjunctive of ἐάω ‘leave alone’, with ἀσινέας ‘unharmed’ agreeing with it; εἰ … κ’ is ‘if’, and μέδηαι, the subjunctive of μέδομαι ‘be mindful of’, takes the genitive νόστου. In the main clause ἦ τ’ ἂν … ἵκοισθε the optative with ἄν is ‘you would reach’, and ἦ is ‘truly’. ἐάᾳς and μέδηαι are singular, ἵκοισθε plural, so Odysseus’s men are included. κακά περ πάσχοντες is ‘though suffering evils’. These lines echo Tiresias’s warning at 11.110–111, with ἦ τ’ ἂν for καί κεν in the second line.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε σίνηαι, τότε τοι τεκμαίρομ’ ὄλεθρον,
νηί τε καὶ ἑτάροις·
sentences.tr:
ei de ke sinēai, tote toi tekmairom’ olethron,
nēi te kai hetarois·
sentences.l:
but if you harm them, then for you I fix destruction,
for ship and companions;
sentences.i: But if you do them harm, then I fix destruction for you, for your ship and your companions;
sentences.n: εἰ … κε with the subjunctive σίνηαι, from σίνομαι ‘harm’, is ‘if you harm them’. τεκμαίρομ’ is τεκμαίρομαι ‘I fix, I mark out as certain’, with ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’ as its object, and νηί and ἑτάροις are datives, ‘for ship and companions’. The two lines are Tiresias’s at 11.112–113, and the English given to them there is kept.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ εἴ πέρ κεν ἀλύξῃς,
ὀψὲ κακῶς νεῖαι, ὀλέσας ἄπο πάντας ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
autos d’ ei per ken alyxēis,
opse kakōs neiai, olesas apo pantas hetairous.
sentences.l:
but you yourself, even if you escape,
late and badly will you come home, having lost all your companions.’
sentences.i: but you yourself, even if you escape, will come home late and in misery, having lost all your companions.’
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘you yourself’ is set against ship and companions. εἴ πέρ κεν ἀλύξῃς is ‘even if you escape’, the subjunctive of ἀλύσκω with περ ‘even’. νεῖαι is the second singular of νέομαι ‘come home’, a present with future sense, and κακῶς ‘badly’ is ‘in misery’. ὀλέσας ἄπο is ἀπολέσας with the preverb standing after its participle (tmesis). Tiresias’s version of the sentence goes on with a further line, ‘on a ship not your own’, which Circe does not repeat. This unit begins in the middle of line 140 and ends her speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτίκα δὲ χρυσόθρονος ἤλυθεν Ἠώς.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autika de chrysothronos ēlythen Ēōs.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and at once golden-throned Dawn came.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and golden-throned Dawn came at once.
sentences.n: The narrator’s line closes Circe’s speech and brings the dawn. χρυσόθρονος ‘golden-throned’ is the stock epithet of Dawn, with an old alternative that derives the second part from θρόνα ‘embroidered flowers’. The whole line occurred at 10.541 and takes its English.

sentences.t: ἡ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀνὰ νῆσον ἀπέστιχε δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: hē men epeit’ ana nēson apestiche dia theaōn·
sentences.l: She then up the island went away, heavenly-one of goddesses;
sentences.i: She then went away up the island, heavenly even among goddesses;
sentences.n: ἡ μέν ‘she on her part’ is answered by αὐτὰρ ἐγών in the next line. ἀνὰ νῆσον is ‘up over the island’, and ἀπέστιχε is the aorist of ἀποστείχω ‘go away’. δῖα θεάων is the stock phrase for Circe, ‘heavenly even among goddesses’, in the house rendering.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐπὶ νῆα κιὼν ὤτρυνον ἑταίρους
αὐτούς τ’ ἀμβαίνειν ἀνά τε πρυμνήσια λῦσαι·
sentences.tr:
autar egōn epi nēa kiōn ōtrynon hetairous
autous t’ ambainein ana te prymnēsia lysai·
sentences.l:
but I, going to the ship, urged on my companions
themselves to embark and to loose the stern-cables;
sentences.i: but I went to the ship and urged my companions themselves to embark and to cast off the stern-cables;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐγών sets Odysseus against Circe; ἐγών is ἐγώ with a movable ν. κιών is the participle of κίω ‘go’, and ὤτρυνον is the imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. ἀμβαίνειν is ἀναβαίνειν ‘to go aboard’, and ἀνά τε … λῦσαι is tmesis for ἀναλῦσαι ‘to loose’. πρυμνήσια are the stern-cables. The second line is the one that stands at 9.178.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ αἶψ’ εἴσβαινον καὶ ἐπὶ κληῖσι καθῖζον.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ aips’ eisbainon kai epi klēisi kathizon.
sentences.l: And they quickly went aboard and on the rowing-benches sat down.
sentences.i: They quickly went aboard and sat down at the oarlocks.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ is ‘and they’. εἴσβαινον is the imperfect of εἰσβαίνω ‘go aboard’, and καθῖζον the imperfect of καθίζω ‘sit down’, the men taking their places one by one. κληῖσι is the dative plural of κληΐς ‘thwart, rowing-bench’, and the plain English keeps the house ‘oarlocks’ for it. The line stood at 11.638 and, with the next line, at 9.103–104, and takes the English given there.

sentences.t: ἑξῆς δ’ ἑζόμενοι πολιὴν ἅλα τύπτον ἐρετμοῖς.
sentences.tr: hexēs d’ hezomenoi poliēn hala typton eretmois.
sentences.l: and sitting in a row, the grey sea they struck with their oars.
sentences.i: and sitting in rows, they struck the grey sea with their oars.
sentences.n: ἑξῆς is ‘in a row, in order’, ἑζόμενοι ‘sitting’, and πολιὴν ἅλα ‘the grey sea’, with the stock epithet. τύπτον is the imperfect of τύπτω ‘strike’, and ἐρετμοῖς the dative ‘with oars’. The line occurs also at 4.580 and 9.104, and keeps its English.

sentences.t:
ἡμῖν δ’ αὖ κατόπισθε νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
ἴκμενον οὖρον ἵει πλησίστιον, ἐσθλὸν ἑταῖρον,
Κίρκη ἐυπλόκαμος, δεινὴ θεὸς αὐδήεσσα.
sentences.tr:
hēmin d’ au katopisthe neos kyanoprōiroio
ikmenon ouron hiei plēsistion, esthlon hetairon,
Kirkē eyplokamos, deinē theos audēessa.
sentences.l:
And for us in turn behind the dark-prowed ship
a favouring wind she sent, sail-filling, a good companion,
Circe, fine-plaited, a dread goddess endowed with speech.
sentences.i: And in her turn, behind our dark-prowed ship, fine-plaited Circe, a dread goddess who speaks with a human voice, sent us a favouring wind that filled the sail, a good companion.
sentences.n: These three lines stand word for word as 11.6–8, and the English there is kept. ἡμῖν δ’ αὖ is ‘and for us in turn’; ἵει is the imperfect of ἵημι ‘send’. ἴκμενον is a rare word whose sense is uncertain, ‘favouring’ being the traditional guess, and πλησίστιον is ‘sail-filling’. For Circe, ἐυπλόκαμος is ‘fine-plaited’, and the force of αὐδήεσσα is debated: the ancient explanation is ‘with a human voice’.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ὅπλα ἕκαστα πονησάμενοι κατὰ νῆα
ἥμεθα·
sentences.tr:
autika d’ hopla hekasta ponēsamenoi kata nēa
hēmetha·
sentences.l:
And at once the gear each piece having worked-at throughout the ship,
we sat;
sentences.i: At once we saw to every piece of gear about the ship and then sat down;
sentences.n: ὅπλα are the ship’s gear, ἕκαστα ‘each thing’, and πονησάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of πονέω ‘labour at, see to’; κατὰ νῆα is ‘throughout the ship’. ἥμεθα is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’. The subject ‘we’ is not expressed. At 11.9 these two lines open with ἡμεῖς δ’ in place of αὐτίκα δ’. The unit ends at the raised point in the middle of line 152.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἄνεμός τε κυβερνήτης τ’ ἴθυνε.
sentences.tr: tēn d’ anemos te kybernētēs t’ ithyne.
sentences.l: and her both the wind and the helmsman steered-straight.
sentences.i: and the wind and the helmsman together kept her on a straight course.
sentences.n: τὴν is the ship, the object of ἴθυνε, the imperfect of ἰθύνω ‘steer straight’; the verb is singular for a double subject, ἄνεμος ‘wind’ and κυβερνήτης ‘helmsman’. Wind and helmsman share the work of keeping her on course. The unit begins in the middle of line 152.

sentences.t: δὴ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἑτάροισι μετηύδων ἀχνύμενος κῆρ·
sentences.tr: dē tot’ egōn hetaroisi metēudōn achnymenos kēr·
sentences.l: Then indeed I among my companions spoke, grieving in heart:
sentences.i: Then, grieving in heart, I spoke among my companions:
sentences.n: δὴ τότ’ is ‘then indeed’. μετηύδων is the first-person imperfect of μεταυδάω ‘speak among’, with ἑτάροισι ‘my companions’, and ἀχνύμενος κῆρ is ‘grieving in heart’, κῆρ being an accusative of respect; the accent on κῆρ ‘heart’ distinguishes it from κήρ ‘doom’ (accusative κῆρα at line 157). A new paragraph: Odysseus now speaks to his men.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐ γὰρ χρὴ ἕνα ἴδμεναι οὐδὲ δύ’ οἴους
θέσφαθ’ ἅ μοι Κίρκη μυθήσατο, δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi, ou gar chrē hena idmenai oude dy’ oious
thesphath’ ha moi Kirkē mythēsato, dia theaōn·
sentences.l:
‘O friends, for it is not right for one to know, nor two alone,
the god-declared things that Circe told me, heavenly-one of goddesses;
sentences.i: ‘Friends, it is not right that only one or two of us should know the prophecies that Circe told me, heavenly even among goddesses;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is ‘friends’. οὐ γὰρ χρή is ‘for it is not right’, taking the infinitive ἴδμεναι, from οἶδα ‘know’ (Attic εἰδέναι), with ἕνα and δύ’ οἴους, ‘one, nor two alone’. θέσφαθ’ is θέσφατα ‘god-declared things, prophecies’, and ἅ μοι Κίρκη μυθήσατο is ‘which Circe told me’, with μυθήσατο unaugmented. In what follows Odysseus first reports Circe’s warning in indirect form (ἀνώγει with infinitives) and then gives his own orders to the crew.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐρέω μὲν ἐγών, ἵνα εἰδότες ἤ κε θάνωμεν
ἤ κεν ἀλευάμενοι θάνατον καὶ κῆρα φύγοιμεν.
sentences.tr:
all’ ereō men egōn, hina eidotes ē ke thanōmen
ē ken aleuamenoi thanaton kai kēra phygoimen.
sentences.l:
but I will tell, I myself, so that knowing, either we may die
or, having avoided death and the death-spirit, we might escape.
sentences.i: but I will tell you myself, so that, knowing, we may either die or avoid death and the death-spirit and escape.
sentences.n: ἐρέω is the future ‘I will tell’, with ἐγών ‘I myself’. ἵνα εἰδότες ἤ κε θάνωμεν ἤ κεν … φύγοιμεν is a purpose clause that changes mood from the subjunctive θάνωμεν to the optative φύγοιμεν: ‘so that, knowing, we may either die or escape’. εἰδότες is the perfect participle of οἶδα. ἀλευάμενοι is the aorist participle of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’, and κῆρα is the accusative of κήρ ‘death-spirit, doom of death’.

sentences.t:
Σειρήνων μὲν πρῶτον ἀνώγει θεσπεσιάων
φθόγγον ἀλεύασθαι καὶ λειμῶν’ ἀνθεμόεντα.
sentences.tr:
Seirēnōn men prōton anōgei thespesiaōn
phthongon aleuasthai kai leimōn’ anthemoenta.
sentences.l:
Of the Sirens first she bade (us) avoid, wondrous ones,
the voice, and the flowery meadow.
sentences.i: First she told us to avoid the voice of the wondrous Sirens, and the flowery meadow.
sentences.n: Σειρήνων … θεσπεσιάων is ‘of the Sirens, the wondrous ones’, with Homer’s -άων for -ῶν. ἀνώγει is the imperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, taking the infinitive ἀλεύασθαι, the aorist of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’; the persons bidden are left out and are ‘us’. φθόγγον is ‘voice, sound’, and λειμῶν’ ἀνθεμόεντα is λειμῶνα ἀνθεμόεντα ‘flowery meadow’. μέν is answered by the next sentence.

sentences.t: οἶον ἔμ’ ἠνώγει ὄπ’ ἀκουέμεν·
sentences.tr: oion em’ ēnōgei op’ akouemen·
sentences.l: Me alone she bade to hear the voice;
sentences.i: She told me alone to hear the voice;
sentences.n: οἶον ἔμ’ is ‘me alone’, οἶον agreeing with ἔμ’ (ἐμέ). ἠνώγει is the augmented form of the verb ἀνώγει of the line before. ὄπ’ is ὄπα, the accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’, and ἀκουέμεν is the infinitive in -έμεν (Attic ἀκούειν). The unit ends at the raised point in the middle of line 160.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με δεσμῷ
δήσατ’ ἐν ἀργαλέῳ, ὄφρ’ ἔμπεδον αὐτόθι μίμνω,
ὀρθὸν ἐν ἱστοπέδῃ, ἐκ δ’ αὐτοῦ πείρατ’ ἀνήφθω.
sentences.tr:
alla me desmōi
dēsat’ en argaleōi, ophr’ empedon autothi mimnō,
orthon en histopedēi, ek d’ autou peirat’ anēphthō.
sentences.l:
but me with a bond
bind, a grievous one, so that firmly right there I stay,
upright in the mast-step, and from it let the rope-ends be fastened.
sentences.i: but bind me in a grievous bond, so that I stay firmly right there, upright in the mast-step, and let the ends of the ropes be fastened from it.
sentences.n: δήσατ’ is the aorist imperative plural of δέω ‘bind’, the order to the crew. δεσμῷ ἐν ἀργαλέῳ is ‘in a grievous bond’, ἀργαλέος keeping its house rendering. ὄφρ’ … μίμνω is a purpose clause with a short-vowel subjunctive of μίμνω ‘remain’; ἔμπεδον is ‘firmly’ and αὐτόθι ‘right there’. ὀρθόν is ‘upright’, ἱστοπέδη the mast-step, and ἀνήφθω the perfect passive imperative of ἀνάπτω ‘fasten’, ‘let it be fastened’. The last line is word for word Circe’s at 12.51.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε λίσσωμαι ὑμέας λῦσαί τε κελεύω,
ὑμεῖς δὲ πλεόνεσσι τότ’ ἐν δεσμοῖσι πιέζειν.
sentences.tr:
ei de ke lissōmai hymeas lysai te keleuō,
hymeis de pleonessi tot’ en desmoisi piezein.
sentences.l:
And if I beg you and bid you to loose me,
you then in more bonds press me.’
sentences.i: And if I beg you and order you to set me free, then press me tight in more bonds.’
sentences.n: εἰ δέ κε … λίσσωμαι … κελεύω is ‘if I beg and order’, two short-vowel subjunctives, with λῦσαι the aorist infinitive of λύω and ὑμέας the Ionic accusative of ὑμεῖς ‘you’. The main verb is the infinitive πιέζειν ‘press’, used as a command as ἐλάαν was; πλεόνεσσι is the epic dative plural of πλείων ‘more’, with δεσμοῖσι ‘bonds’. This ends Odysseus’s speech to his men.

sentences.t: ἦ τοι ἐγὼ τὰ ἕκαστα λέγων ἑτάροισι πίφαυσκον·
sentences.tr: ē toi egō ta hekasta legōn hetaroisi piphauskon·
sentences.l: Indeed I, each thing telling, to my companions kept declaring;
sentences.i: So I told my companions every detail, making it known to them;
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the narrator takes up the voyage again. ἦ τοι is ‘so then’, and τὰ ἕκαστα is ‘each thing’. λέγων is ‘telling’, and πίφαυσκον is the imperfect of πιφαύσκω ‘make known’, a present with reduplication; the imperfect means he kept on explaining.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δὲ καρπαλίμως ἐξίκετο νηῦς ἐυεργὴς
νῆσον Σειρήνοιιν·
sentences.tr:
tophra de karpalimōs exiketo nēus eyergēs
nēson Seirēnoiin·
sentences.l:
and meanwhile speedily came the well-made ship
to the island of the two Sirens;
sentences.i: meanwhile the well-made ship came speedily to the island of the two Sirens;
sentences.n: τόφρα is ‘meanwhile’. καρπαλίμως is ‘speedily’, ἐξίκετο the aorist of ἐξικνέομαι ‘reach’, and νηῦς ἐυεργής ‘the well-made ship’. Σειρήνοιιν is the genitive dual ‘of the two Sirens’, ending in -οιιν. The unit ends at the raised point in the middle of line 167.

sentences.t: ἔπειγε γὰρ οὖρος ἀπήμων.
sentences.tr: epeige gar ouros apēmōn.
sentences.l: for was urging on a fair wind, harmless.
sentences.i: for a harmless fair wind was driving her on.
sentences.n: ἔπειγε is the imperfect of ἐπείγω ‘press on, urge’, and γάρ gives the reason for the speed. οὖρος ἀπήμων is ‘a harmless fair wind’; ἀπήμων is ‘without woe’, from πῆμα. The unit begins in the middle of line 167.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτ’ ἄνεμος μὲν ἐπαύσατο ἠδὲ γαλήνη
ἔπλετο νηνεμίη, κοίμησε δὲ κύματα δαίμων.
sentences.tr:
autik’ epeit’ anemos men epausato ēde galēnē
epleto nēnemiē, koimēse de kymata daimōn.
sentences.l:
At once then the wind ceased, and a calm
became windlessness, and the waves lulled to sleep some power.
sentences.i: At once the wind dropped, and a windless calm came, and some power lulled the waves to sleep.
sentences.n: μέν is answered by the δέ in the second line. ἐπαύσατο is the aorist middle of παύω ‘cease’, and ἔπλετο the aorist of πέλομαι ‘became’, unaugmented. νηνεμίη is ‘windlessness’, standing beside γαλήνη ‘calm’. κοίμησε is the aorist of κοιμάω ‘lull to sleep’. δαίμων is ‘some power’; the Greek names no god.

sentences.t:
ἀνστάντες δ’ ἕταροι νεὸς ἱστία μηρύσαντο
καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν νηὶ γλαφυρῇ θέσαν, οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ἐρετμὰ
ἑζόμενοι λεύκαινον ὕδωρ ξεστῇς ἐλάτῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
anstantes d’ hetaroi neos histia mērysanto
kai ta men en nēi glaphyrēi thesan, hoi d’ ep’ eretma
hezomenoi leukainon hydōr xestēis elatēisin.
sentences.l:
And having stood up, my companions the ship’s sails furled
and those in the hollow ship put, but they to the oars
sitting whitened the water with polished fir-oars.
sentences.i: My companions stood up and furled the ship’s sails and put them away in the hollow ship, and sitting down at the oars they whitened the water with their polished fir-oars.
sentences.n: ἀνστάντες is ἀναστάντες ‘having stood up’, and ἕταροι is a metrical variant of ἑταῖροι. μηρύσαντο is the aorist middle of μηρύομαι ‘furl’. τὰ μέν ‘those’, the sails, is set against οἱ δέ ‘but they’, the men. θέσαν is the aorist of τίθημι. λεύκαινον is the imperfect of λευκαίνω ‘whiten’, and ἐλάτῃσιν the dative of ἐλάτη ‘fir’, then ‘oar’ made of it, with ξεστῇς ‘polished’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ κηροῖο μέγαν τροχὸν ὀξέι χαλκῷ
τυτθὰ διατμήξας χερσὶ στιβαρῇσι πίεζον·
sentences.tr:
autar egō kēroio megan trochon oxei chalkōi
tyttha diatmēxas chersi stibarēisi piezon·
sentences.l:
But I a great wheel of wax with the sharp bronze
in small pieces having cut, with sturdy hands pressed it;
sentences.i: But I cut a great round of wax into small pieces with the sharp bronze, and pressed it in my sturdy hands;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐγώ marks the change to Odysseus himself. κηροῖο is the genitive of κηρός ‘wax’, and τροχόν ‘wheel’ here means a big round of it. ὀξέι χαλκῷ is ‘with sharp bronze’, a bronze blade. τυτθά is an adverbial neuter plural ‘in small bits’, διατμήξας the aorist participle of διατμήγω ‘cut through’, and στιβαρῇσι ‘sturdy’. πίεζον is the imperfect of πιέζω ‘press’: he worked it in his hands.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἰαίνετο κηρός, ἐπεὶ κέλετο μεγάλη ἲς
Ἠελίου τ’ αὐγὴ Ὑπεριονίδαο ἄνακτος·
sentences.tr:
aipsa d’ iaineto kēros, epei keleto megalē is
Ēeliou t’ augē Hyperionidao anaktos·
sentences.l:
and soon the wax was warmed, since urged on the great force
and the ray of the Sun, Hyperion’s son, the lord;
sentences.i: and the wax soon grew warm, for the great force and ray of the lord Sun, the son of Hyperion, drove it on;
sentences.n: ἰαίνετο is the imperfect of ἰαίνω ‘warm, soften’, and αἶψα is ‘soon’. κέλετο is the imperfect middle of κέλομαι ‘urge’, with two subjects, ἲς ‘force’ and αὐγή ‘ray’, the sun’s heat doing what the hands began. Ὑπεριονίδαο ἄνακτος, ‘the lord, son of Hyperion’, stands in apposition to Ἠελίου. The unit ends at the raised point at the end of line 176.

sentences.t: ἑξείης δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἐπ’ οὔατα πᾶσιν ἄλειψα.
sentences.tr: hexeiēs d’ hetaroisin ep’ ouata pasin aleipsa.
sentences.l: and in order on the ears of all my companions I smeared (it).
sentences.i: and one after another I smeared it on the ears of all my companions.
sentences.n: ἑξείης is ‘in order, one after another’. ἑτάροισιν … πᾶσιν is ‘all my companions’, and ἐπ’ οὔατα ‘onto the ears’, οὔατα being Homer’s plural of οὖς. ἄλειψα is the aorist of ἀλείφω ‘smear’, with the wax understood as its object. This does what Circe told him to do to the crew’s ears at 12.47–48.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐν νηί μ’ ἔδησαν ὁμοῦ χεῖράς τε πόδας τε
ὀρθὸν ἐν ἱστοπέδῃ, ἐκ δ’ αὐτοῦ πείρατ’ ἀνῆπτον·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ en nēi m’ edēsan homou cheiras te podas te
orthon en histopedēi, ek d’ autou peirat’ anēpton·
sentences.l:
And they in the ship bound me, together hands and feet,
upright in the mast-step, and from it the rope-ends fastened;
sentences.i: And they bound me in the ship, hands and feet together, upright in the mast-step, and fastened the ends of the ropes from it;
sentences.n: The order of 160–162 is now carried out. οἱ δέ is ‘and they’, ἔδησαν the aorist of δέω ‘bind’, and ὁμοῦ ‘together’. The second line is that of 162 and 12.51, with the imperfect ἀνῆπτον ‘they fastened’ where the commands had the imperative ἀνήφθω. The unit ends at the raised point.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ δ’ ἑζόμενοι πολιὴν ἅλα τύπτον ἐρετμοῖς.
sentences.tr: autoi d’ hezomenoi poliēn hala typton eretmois.
sentences.l: and they themselves, sitting, the grey sea struck with oars.
sentences.i: and they themselves sat down and struck the grey sea with their oars.
sentences.n: αὐτοί is ‘they themselves’, the crew, after the account of what was done to Odysseus. The line is the one at 147, with αὐτοὶ δ’ in place of ἑξῆς δ’; πολιὴν ἅλα is ‘the grey sea’, with the stock epithet, and τύπτον ἐρετμοῖς ‘struck with oars’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε τόσσον ἀπῆμεν ὅσον τε γέγωνε βοήσας,
ῥίμφα διώκοντες, τὰς δ’ οὐ λάθεν ὠκύαλος νηῦς
ἐγγύθεν ὀρνυμένη, λιγυρὴν δ’ ἔντυνον ἀοιδήν·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote tosson apēmen hoson te gegōne boēsas,
rhimpha diōkontes, tas d’ ou lathen ōkyalos nēus
engythen ornymenē, ligyrēn d’ entynon aoidēn·
sentences.l:
But when so far we were away as one is heard who has shouted,
nimbly driving on, them the swift-sailing ship did not escape,
rushing from close by, and a clear song they set going:
sentences.i: But when we were as far off as a man’s shout carries, driving on nimbly, the swift-sailing ship did not escape their notice as it rushed up close, and they set up a clear song:
sentences.n: τόσσον … ὅσον τε γέγωνε βοήσας is ‘as far as one is heard who shouts’, γέγωνε being a perfect with present sense and βοήσας the aorist participle of βοάω. ἀπῆμεν is the imperfect of ἄπειμι ‘be away’. τὰς are the Sirens, accusative after οὐ λάθεν ‘did not escape’, and νηῦς is the subject; ὠκύαλος is ‘swift-sailing’, from ὠκύς and ἅλς. ῥίμφα διώκοντες is ‘driving on nimbly’. The subject then changes to the Sirens: ἔντυνον is the imperfect of ἐντύνω ‘set going’.

sentences.t:
δεῦρ’ ἄγ’ ἰών, πολύαιν’ Ὀδυσεῦ, μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν,
νῆα κατάστησον, ἵνα νωιτέρην ὄπ ἀκούσῃς.
sentences.tr:
deur’ ag’ iōn, polyain’ Odyseu, mega kydos Achaiōn,
nēa katastēson, hina nōiterēn op akousēis.
sentences.l:
‘Here, come, going on, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans,
bring the ship to a stand, so that of us two the voice you may hear.
sentences.i: ‘Come here, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans, bring your ship to a halt, so that you may hear the voice of the two of us.
sentences.n: The Sirens speak. δεῦρ’ ἄγ’ ἰών is ‘hither, come, going on’. πολύαιν’ is πολύαινε, ‘much-praised’, built on πολύς and αἶνος ‘praise’, and μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν ‘great glory of the Achaeans’ also addresses Nestor at 3.79. κατάστησον is the aorist imperative of καθίστημι ‘bring to a stand’. νωιτέρην is the dual possessive ‘belonging to us two’, and ὄπ is ὄπα ‘voice’, printed here without the elision mark.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πώ τις τῇδε παρήλασε νηὶ μελαίνῃ,
πρίν γ’ ἡμέων μελίγηρυν ἀπὸ στομάτων ὄπ’ ἀκοῦσαι,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε τερψάμενος νεῖται καὶ πλείονα εἰδώς.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō tis tēide parēlase nēi melainēi,
prin g’ hēmeōn meligēryn apo stomatōn op’ akousai,
all’ ho ge terpsamenos neitai kai pleiona eidōs.
sentences.l:
For no one yet by this way has sailed past in a black ship
before from our mouths a honey-toned voice he has heard,
but he, having delighted himself, goes on his way, and knowing more.
sentences.i: For no one has yet sailed past here in a black ship without first hearing the honey-toned voice from our mouths; but he goes on his way delighted, and knowing more.
sentences.n: τῇδε is ‘this way, here’, and παρήλασε the aorist of παρελαύνω ‘drive past’, here ‘sail past’. πρίν γ’ … ἀκοῦσαι is ‘before hearing’, πρίν with the aorist infinitive. ἡμέων is the Ionic form of ἡμῶν ‘of us’, and μελίγηρυν ‘honey-toned’ is built on μέλι ‘honey’ and γῆρυς ‘voice’; ὄπ’ is ὄπα. τερψάμενος is ‘having delighted himself’, νεῖται ‘goes on his way’, from νέομαι, and πλείονα εἰδώς ‘knowing more’.

sentences.t:
ἴδμεν γάρ τοι πάνθ’ ὅσ’ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ εὐρείῃ
Ἀργεῖοι Τρῶές τε θεῶν ἰότητι μόγησαν,
ἴδμεν δ’, ὅσσα γένηται ἐπὶ χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ.
sentences.tr:
idmen gar toi panth’ hos’ eni Troiēi eureiēi
Argeioi Trōes te theōn iotēti mogēsan,
idmen d’, hossa genētai epi chthoni poulyboteirēi.
sentences.l:
For we know all that in Troy broad
the Argives and the Trojans through the will of gods toiled,
and we know whatever may come to pass on the much-nourishing earth.’
sentences.i: For we know everything that the Argives and the Trojans toiled through in broad Troy by the will of the gods, and we know whatever happens on the earth that feeds so many.’
sentences.n: ἴδμεν is the first plural of οἶδα ‘we know’ (Attic ἴσμεν), and τοι is ‘I tell you’. πάνθ’ ὅσ’ is ‘all that’, and μόγησαν the aorist of μογέω ‘toil’; θεῶν ἰότητι is ‘by the will of the gods’. ὅσσα γένηται is an indefinite relative clause with the subjunctive, ‘whatever comes to pass’, and πουλυβοτείρῃ is the stock epithet ‘much-nourishing’. This closes the Sirens’ speech: the narrator’s line at 192 follows, so the English closes the single mark here.
